Photos, Video and Marketing
Introduction
Today, the first visit to your property happens on a screen. Quality photos and marketing determine who books a viewing — and who moves on. Marketing isn't a luxury: it's what fills your showings.
This guide covers photos, video, the description and distribution, to maximize attention and attract the right buyers.
Each chapter ends with a lined “My notes” page.

Today, a sale is won first online: photos, video, description and distribution decide whether the buyer clicks or scrolls past. This guide covers every marketing lever, from preparing the space to reaching the right audience.
The principle: tend to the digital storefront as much as the property itself.
Photos: your digital storefront
Understanding why photos make (or break) the sale.
Understanding why photos make (or break) the sale.

Buyers judge your property in a few seconds from the photos. Bright, sharp, well-framed images generate more clicks, more visits and better offers. Dark or amateur photos do the opposite, even for a beautiful property.
Professional photos: light, controlled wide-angle, a prepared property (staging).
A logical order and a strong lead photo (often the façade or the feature room).
Enough of them: show all the key rooms without misleading.

Buyers judge in a few seconds, on the photos, before they even read the description. Professional, bright, well-framed photos make the difference between “let's visit” and “skip”. It's the most profitable marketing investment of a sale.
Emilie's tip
Never skimp on photos: it's the highest-return investment of the entire sale. A well-prepared, poorly photographed property sells for less than it should.
Video and the virtual tour
Going beyond the photo to stand out.
Going beyond the photo to stand out.

Video and the virtual tour (3D tour, floor plans) let buyers picture themselves before travelling. They attract serious buyers, including those coming from farther away, and filter out less relevant visits.
A short, dynamic video showcasing the flow and the atmosphere.
A virtual tour to explore at one's own pace.
A floor plan to understand the volumes.

Video and the virtual tour (3D, floor plans) let buyers picture themselves and filter before travelling: you get more qualified visitors. For out-of-area buyers, it's often what triggers the first in-person visit.
Emilie's tip
Video tells the atmosphere and lifestyle that a photo freezes. For a property with strong character (view, layout, area), it's a powerful trigger of emotion and visits.
The description that makes people want in
Writing copy that sells without misleading.
Writing copy that sells without misleading.
Open on asset #1 (location, light, renovation, yard).
Describe the spaces concretely and the benefits (not just dimensions).
Mention the neighbourhood and its amenities.
Stay honest: a misleading description creates disappointed visits and offers that fall through.

A good description opens on asset #1 (location, light, renovation, yard), describes concretely without exaggerating, and ends with a call to action. It sells without misleading: promising what you can't deliver generates disappointed visits and offers that collapse.
Emilie's tip
Sell the benefits, not just the features: not “a 12-foot kitchen”, but “a light-filled kitchen made for entertaining”. The buyer buys a life, not dimensions.
Distribution: being seen by the right buyers
Maximizing exposure to the right audience.
Maximizing exposure to the right audience.
Wide distribution: Centris, portals, social media, the broker network.
Targeting: putting the property in front of the area's active buyers.
Launch momentum: concentrating exposure in the first weeks, when interest is highest.
Sign, open houses and QR codes to also capture local buyers.
A large part of a broker's value lies in this network and distribution machine, hard to replicate on your own.

Distribution must aim wide AND accurately: Centris, portals, social media, the network of contacts and buyers. A beautiful property poorly distributed sells poorly; exposure to the right audience is as important as the quality of the visuals.
Emilie's tip
Tend to the launch: focus the marketing energy on the first two weeks. That's the window when interest is strongest and where your best offers often play out.

Treat photo day like a demanding buyer's visit: everything must be tidy, clean and bright. The photos are your first impression online, and there's only one.

Virtual tour: a 3D walkthrough allowing a remote visit.
Digital curb appeal: photo quality that makes people want to visit.
Call to action: a clear invitation to visit or make an offer.
